title: Unified Uncertainty Quantification Framework Bridging Noisy Quantum Backends Across Variational Quantum Algorithms and Quantum Signal Processing
authors: Priyabrata Senapati, Vibin Abraham, Qiang Guan, Bo Peng
abstract: We present an uncertainty quantification (UQ) framework for application level benchmarking and characterization of noisy quantum backends. The framework compares two workload classes under one statistical pipeline: noisy intermediate scale quantum (NISQ) variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) and Quantum Singular Value Transformation (QSVT) based Green's function reconstruction. For the VQA branch, we evaluate ten benchmark families spanning chemistry, optimization, simulation, compiling, linear solving, partial differential equations, metrology, error correction, tomography, and channel fidelity estimation. For the QSVT branch, we reconstruct orbital resolved Green's functions and spectral peaks from a block encoded real time propagator. The workflow combines Bayesian optimization, posterior distribution refinement, sensitivity analysis, robust parameter density estimation, backend ranking, noise correlation, and resource estimation analysis. Instead of reporting only one best parameter vector, the framework identifies robust parameter regions, residual gaps to ideal behavior, backend specific failure modes, and calibration sensitive uncertainty. The result is a common benchmark for variational and non-variational workloads that measures how reliably each backend reaches useful task level behavior.
summary: This paper introduces a unified Uncertainty Quantification framework designed to benchmark noisy quantum computers across diverse computational tasks. By integrating Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) and Green's function reconstruction via QSVT, it moves beyond simple hardware metrics. The resulting common benchmark quantifies the reliability of backends to achieve useful task-level results.
main_problem: To develop a unified Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) framework for application-level benchmarking of noisy quantum backends, bridging Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) and non-variational methods like QSVT.
main_result: The framework provides a common benchmark that measures how reliably different quantum backends can achieve useful task-level behavior across diverse workloads, identifying robust parameter regions and failure modes.
method: It combines Bayesian optimization with posterior distribution refinement to quantify uncertainty for both VQA objective functions and Green's function reconstructions derived via QSVT.
model_or_system: The work evaluates performance on NISQ quantum hardware backends using two primary workload classes: general variational tasks (chemistry, optimization, PDEs) and spectral reconstruction from time-propagators (Green's functions).
key_observables: Backend rankings across workloads, robust parameter regions geometry, residual gaps to ideal behavior, mean regret trajectories, and quality vs. speed Pareto frontiers.
important_parameters: The workload parameters ($\vec{\lambda}$) defining the task observable $\mathcal{O}_w$, the optimization parameters ($ oldsymbol{	heta}$), and the noise characteristics of the quantum backend.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on IBM fake backend noise models instead of live QPUs, and assumes that a single statistical interface can unify both variational and non-variational workloads for consistent comparison.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate shared UQ workflows connecting VQA and QSVT branches; they show cross-backend sensitivity summaries (Morris/SHAP), density maps of robust parameter regions, and application-level performance comparisons (Pareto views).
paper_structure: The paper introduces the unified UQ framework by first defining the two workload classes (VQA and QSVT) and then detailing the combined methodology. It presents results comparing backend performance across multiple domains using sensitivity analysis and optimization convergence metrics.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, quantitative method to benchmark quantum hardware beyond simple gate fidelity, directly assessing if the noise profile allows for meaningful physical conclusions in complex applications like many-body physics or chemistry.
